chapter_theme: The buffalo killed by the king's men for the loss of a horse is eaten by Amirthamathi, who is then struck by leprosy, which onlookers call the fruit of her deeds; one who understands visits and reproaches her, and the soul is born as a cock that the king has reared, while the chapter closes on the spring.

205.reading: The verse lists the rebirths so far (Chandramathi a dog, a black snake after) and says that the one now followed came to the goods-rich land of Kalinga as a buffalo and grew up there.
205.nuance: The line 'வாடது' and who the snake is are hard; that the buffalo is the poisoned king reborn is taken from the sequel (the queen's eating of it, 212, and the accusation at 221), not stated in the verse.
205.event: The one passing through rebirths is born and grows as a buffalo in Kalinga.

206.reading: The buffalo travels with merchants, bearing their goods without rest, and one day the merchants halt their caravan outside Ujjain by the river.
206.event: Merchants and their burden-buffalo come and camp on the bank beside Ujjain.

207.reading: Wearied by the load it carried, the buffalo runs into the Sipra river, bathes its fill, and coming to the bank it strikes the horse that has come there.
207.nuance: The word மா in line 4 is read here as 'horse', since 208 names the royal mount as lost; the edition leaves it as 'the animal'.
207.event: The buffalo, freed of its load, bathes in the Sipra and gores a horse on the bank.

208.reading: The king's attendants announce that the royal mount named Arasavannam, killed by the merchants' buffalo, is gone.
208.nuance: The attendants lay the loss on the merchants through their buffalo, which sets up the king's seizure in 209.
208.event: The royal attendants report to the king that his horse is dead through the merchants' buffalo.

209.reading: The king, in a rage, orders the merchants' wealth and the buffalo seized and brought to him, and his men go and carry off goods past counting.
209.nuance: The verse itself does not condemn; the claim is the reader's reading of the report. The king is unnamed here; he is taken to be Yasomati by the story so far.
209.event: The king orders the merchants' goods and the buffalo taken, and his men plunder them.

claims.claim: a king who answers one animal's act by plundering the merchants who owned it is not guarding his people

210.reading: The merciless men, knowing the king's order, bind the beast's four feet and strip it of all its means, leaving it with only dharma as its fortress.
210.nuance: சரணம் நான்கு can be 'four feet' or the four refuges of Jain practice; the first is followed here, and the line 'only dharma is its fortress' may carry the second meaning.
210.event: The king's men bind and disable the buffalo as ordered.

211.reading: The buffalo is killed in stages: boiled in caustic water, cut apart, its belly emptied, a rod stirred through ghee, and at last it is finished with a thorn-sharp whip.
211.nuance: The step-by-step account of the butchery is a Jain teaching device: the pain of the animal is set out so that the later eating of its flesh (212) is felt as cruelty.
211.event: The king's men slaughter and prepare the buffalo with cruelty.

claims.claim: the slaughter of a creature for the table is a long torment to it

212.reading: The queen, a vine of a woman named Amirthamathi, puts the well-cooked buffalo flesh in her mouth and fattens her belly; the others say she is working some illusion.
212.nuance: The queen is Yasodharan's wife and, if the buffalo is the poisoned king reborn (205 and 221 suggest it), she is eating her victim; the verse does not say this, the sequel does.
212.event: Amirthamathi eats the cooked flesh of the buffalo while others comment.

claims.claim: eating the flesh of a slaughtered creature feeds only the body and brings its own fruit

213.reading: The queen says she still has hunger, that a ram lives close by, and that biting its thigh and eating it today would put her craving to an end.
213.nuance: Her words show appetite growing as it is fed; the epic's own voice holds the opposite, that craving is not ended by eating.
213.event: Amirthamathi asks for a ram to be killed so she may eat its thigh.

claims.claim: eating the flesh of an animal ends craving

214.reading: The verse looks back: in anger she took the life of the great lord whose beauty matched Kama's, mixing his poison with her passion, and joined a man she had made a human dog.
214.nuance: 'Human dog' is the narrator's contempt for the man, not a name; the earlier chapters name him Ashtavakran (ch.6).
214.event: Recalled: Amirthamathi poisons her husband and takes the hunchback as her lover.

claims.claim: desire joined to hatred can lead a wife to kill her husband

215.reading: After she had sported with the low-born hunchback of leprous body, a day comes when one of beautiful frame, now spoiled, is plunged in leprosy.
215.nuance: மேனியன் in line 3 is masculine, while 216 uses feminine forms for the sufferer; the sense is taken as the queen, but the form could point at the hunchback.
215.event: Amirthamathi falls ill with leprosy after her years with Ashtavakran.

216.reading: Her limbs rot and wither, she oozes sores, flies crowd in the stench, and many more diseases gather upon her.
216.event: Leprosy and other diseases ravage Amirthamathi's body.

217.reading: Those who see her say that she has no understanding by the strong karma of a former birth, that this is the fruit of what she did in this birth, and that this karma does not lie, and does not die even if she dies.
217.nuance: The speakers are named in 219 only as those who said this behind her back; 'எம்மையும்' (us too) is hard to place.

claims.claim: deeds of an earlier birth and of this one ripen on the doer
karma does not perish with the body

218.reading: They wonder whether it was craving for the disease, want of fine discernment, or the gathering of heavy evil karma that made her eat the dead buffalo, and say this delusion will seize her again.

claims.claim: craving and want of fine discernment lead one to gather evil karma

219.reading: So they spoke behind her back; then one who fully understood it all went to see her, pained in mind.
219.nuance: The word வத்தகர் is obscure and who the visitor is is not fixed by the Tamil; 220 and 221 let him be the man she poisoned.
219.event: Her attendants speak, and one who understood goes to see her.

220.reading: The visitor reproaches the queen: she was angry at him, she went and delighted in a sinner, and now her body is thus and she has seized him too.
220.nuance: 'Sinner' (பாவி) is used for her lover, for her, and for the speaker's own fate, so the verse is open to two readings of who has seized whom.

claims.claim: delight in a sinner brings bodily ruin as its fruit

221.reading: The visitor says she tormented him with his mother by poison, that her wrath has not ended though she is dying, and asks whether, with the buffalo lying in her belly, she will plot against him too.
221.nuance: This is the verse that makes the visitor the poisoned king; the buffalo here is a third party, 'that buffalo' in her belly, so whether the buffalo is he or his mother is left open.
221.event: The visitor accuses the queen of the poison and of the eaten buffalo.

222.reading: Seeing her so, he asks what reproach can do; one thing still burns in his heart, and the life undone by the queen's torment went on its way with the buffalo.
222.nuance: Whether the life that goes with the buffalo is the queen's or the visitor's is not settled by the grammar.

claims.claim: reproach does not mend a deed already ripened

223.reading: In that great city, in a Paraiya street of small houses and many people, the soul takes the form of a cock, and the victorious spear-king wishes to see it.
223.nuance: The street is named only as the place of the birth; the verse does not judge the birth by it.
223.event: The soul is born as a cock and the king wants to see it.

224.reading: The king is delighted at the sight and orders Chandakarmi to be given charge to raise it; he takes it to his cage and rears it, and it grows skilled in war.
224.nuance: This Chandakarmi is a cock-keeper, whom the Tamil does not equate with the Chandakarman who brought the youths in ch.2 and 3.
224.event: The king has the cock reared by Chandakarmi, who trains it for fighting.

225.reading: The cock grows, its eyes like pearls, its wings like a bow, its crest bright like a gem-crown, its golden feet with diamond spurs matchless in battle, and its strength unflagging.

226.reading: The grove with its red shoots, bees, honey and koel calls fills with the south wind, and the heart rejoices everywhere in the season of honey.

links.note: The onlookers name the fruit of a woman's cruelty as leprosy, coming to her body; the couplet says only that harm returns of itself.
links.teaches: The epic shows the return of harm as a long delay in which the doer is first shown eating and then rotting, which the couplet's afternoon-for-forenoon image cannot show.

gains.a: the unit gains a plain rule that harm to others comes back to the doer, without needing a past birth
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the return takes years, passes through a body and is read by onlookers as karma

links.note: Both say a deed finds its doer; the epic adds that it outlasts her death.
links.teaches: Putting 217 beside the calf-and-mother image shows that the Jain epic makes the deed's claim reach past the doer's body, a step the quatrain does not take.

gains.a: the unit gains an image of how the old deed finds her, as a calf picks out its mother
gains.b: the quatrain gains a limit case, where the deed still stands after the body has failed

links.note: Amirthamathi once defended her fortune as the fruit of an earlier deed; the same law now explains her disease.
links.teaches: The queen's own argument for her desire turns on her: she cited former deeds as the source of what one has, and her sickness is that source's other side.

links.note: The king reasoned that desire wastes the body and fame; the queen's body is wasted.
links.teaches: His reasoning from the night of the tryst is borne out on her body, which turns a private resolve into a visible fact.

links.note: The Siddhar's woman is a pit of sores by nature; here the sores come on one woman as the result of what she did.
links.teaches: The epic places the body's foulness in a deed and its time, where the Siddhar places it in woman's nature, so the two verses disagree on its cause.

gains.a: the unit gains a rival account of the foul body in which the foulness is a lure, not a punishment
gains.b: the song gains a case that says the sores follow a deed, which unsettles blaming woman as such

links.note: The couplet says sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; here a wife crosses, and the fruit falls on her.
links.teaches: The couplet is spoken to a man; the epic carries the same four ills onto a wife and adds the one the couplet lacks, the disease of her own body.

gains.a: the unit gains a stated rule that the crossing carries its own ruin
gains.b: the couplet gains a woman as the one who crosses, and a bodily fruit beyond blame

links.note: The couplet asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can hold to compassion; here the flesh is possibly her victim's.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's general 'another creature' into a creature that may be her own victim's next body, which sharpens its question.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that eating flesh is a failure of compassion in itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the flesh may belong to someone she wronged

links.note: Tirumular puts the flesh-eaters' pain in hell, after death; the epic spends its verses on the animal's pain first.
links.teaches: The epic puts the pain first on the animal and sets the eater's suffering later in this same life, where Tirumular's punishment lies only after death.

gains.a: the unit gains a Saiva voice that also holds flesh-eating to be punished
gains.b: the verse gains the animal's side of the pain, which it does not describe

links.note: The couplet calls a king who torments his people crueller than a killer; here the king seizes merchants' goods over a horse.
links.teaches: The epic's king acts from a sudden anger, not from habit, so it shows how the couplet's cruelty can come from one incident and an unexamined report.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule by which the seizure can be called cruelty
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of tyranny arising from one angry order, not a settled vice

links.note: The earlier king calls a king the shield of all living beings; this king's order falls on merchants and an animal.
links.teaches: One king's rule that a ruler guards every life is set against his successor's order that brings pain on innocent persons and a beast.

cast.role: the buffalo of the merchants, the next rebirth of the one the story follows; identity from the sequel
the merchants whose buffalo kills the royal horse
the king's attendants who report the horse's death and carry out his order
the king of Ujjain, unnamed in these verses; Yasodharan's son by the story so far
Yasodharan's widow, who poisoned him and eats the buffalo's flesh
the others who say she is working an illusion
those who speak behind the queen's back; named only in 219
the one who goes to see the leprous queen; by 221 the man she poisoned, but the Tamil does not say
the cock into which the soul is born
the cock-keeper to whom the king gives the cock

source_issues: Verse 205 is hard in its second and third lines (வாடது) and who is the snake is unclear.
Verse 207 line 4 'மா' is read as 'horse' from 208, not stated.
Verse 210 சரணம் may be feet or the four refuges.
Verse 215 மேனியன் is masculine where the sense is the queen; compare 216.
Verse 219 வத்தகர் is obscure; who the visitor is is inferred.
Verses 220 to 222 leave speakers and the person who goes with the buffalo open.
